submission.natural_language_explanation: Neuron 1829's preactivation encodes the definiteness of the noun phrase being read: it is strongly positive (+0.5 to +1.2) inside definite or presuppositional reference ('the', 'this/these/those', possessives, 'each/every/all/both/most', 'of the X'), and strongly negative (-0.6 to -1.3) inside indefinite, quantified or comparative phrasing ('a/an X', 'some/any/no/several/other/another X', bare numerals, 'more/less/similar/different X'). The negative pole is the GELU dip of that signal, so its strength rises as the preactivation falls from 0, reaches the 0.17 ceiling where the preactivation sits near GELU's minimum of -0.75 (typically the token right after an indefinite article, or a mildly indefinite clause), stays at about 0 only where the whole text is definite/specific (prepositions, bare time nouns and generic verbs still dip below the activity line even there), and falls back to 0.05-0.10 where the preactivation drops past about -1.3 (heavily quantified text such as 'several ... several ...').

rival_explanations: It is a degree/comparison neuron rather than a definiteness one: it fires on quantitative or comparative description ('more', 'less', 'similar', 'different', 'several', gradable adjectives) and its article contrast is incidental, so 'The bigger car won the race' should fire as strongly as 'A bigger car won the race'.

It is a lexical n-gram detector on the preceding determiner word: it fires whenever the literal tokens 'a', 'an', 'some', 'several', 'other' or a numeral appear in the last few tokens and is blind to definiteness marked any other way, so possessives, demonstratives, 'each/every/all' and bare plurals should leave it quiet and 'such a thing' should fire.

It is a number/token-identity detector: the pole fires on numerals and a fixed set of frequent function tokens (' 1971', '0000', 'and', ')', '%'), so a text's peak is predicted by the presence of those tokens rather than by definiteness, and 'The results were similar' should be quiet while any numeral-containing sentence fires.

How can marketers measure email effectiveness more accurately, and what implications does this have for securing digital investment? Answer according to: Eagle-eyed Econsultancy readers will notice that we’ve published a number of end-of-year roundups recently.
For each of these posts we asked a panel of experts for their views, and while I had their attention I slipped in a few extra questions.
So, what did our marketing experts think was the most common mistake that brands still make with their email campaigns, and in an ideal world what would they like to see happen to email marketing in 2016?
And for more on this topic, read our post looking at email trends for 2016 or read our Email Marketing Census 2015.
What is the most common error that brands still make with email marketing?
Getting personalisation wrong. When it’s great it’s brilliant, but be warned when it’s used badly the user experience is terrible.
Marketers need to be careful not to make too many assumptions.
Also, emails that are not optimised for the mobile user journey (this is expected).
Asking for preferences but then not delivering based on the answers – if you are going to ask you have to be prepared to take action, regardless of what the answer is.
I continue to be amazed by the number of email marketers I work with who can’t measure the value of their own programs.
We’ve seen research that suggests almost 50% of email marketers aren’t confident they can calculate ROI from their activities.
This has some real implications – how do these marketers justify having an email program to their stakeholders if they can’t assign a value to it?
Also, the inability to measure ROI is one of the top-three barriers to securing digital investment.
Most brands measure email effectiveness based upon last-click attribution models, and this is a bad idea.
Think about your own experience – when’s the last time you got an email from Amazon, opened it, clicked on it, and then bought something there and then?
Remember that email is also – and importantly – a branding channel, regardless of next-steps, and email engagement surely drives the nefarious ‘direct traffic’ that delivers a huge percentage of conversions.
So I hope that in 2016 brands will realise that, while sales from email is great, the ‘brand halo’ effect from frequent, effective emails is the real value of an email database.
Last-click is so 2015, so let’s move on.
Being afraid to experiment and test their strategy.
We all love best practice and stellar examples of email marketing as inspiration for our own communications, but at the end of the day each brand’s audience is unique.
Just because something worked well a few years ago, it doesn’t mean there is no other winning strategy.
Let the data show you the way, and don’t be afraid to experiment with new tactics and technologies.

2. Background Art
An optical disk, such as CD-R (recordable CD), DVD±R (recordable DVD), BD-R (write-once type Blu-ray Disc), or the like, has a structure that a recording layer and a reflective layer (and a protection layer as needed) are formed on one surface of an optically transparent disk-shaped substrate. Furthermore, spiral or concentric grooves called as grooves are formed on the surface of the substrate on which the recording layer and the reflective layer are formed, and a projecting portion called as a land is formed between neighboring grooves. With respect to the optical disk as described above, the recording layer on a groove is irradiated with a recording laser beam to form pits, thereby performing recording. The length of the pit, the length of the portion between the pits (hereinafter referred to as a space) and the arrangement of the pits are readout by applying a reproduction laser beam and detecting a reflective light as a reproduction signal, thereby performing reproduction.
With respect to the optical disk as described above, the recording layer is irradiated through an optically transparent layer with the recording laser beam and the reproducing laser beam. Here, in the case of CD-R or DVD±R, the recording layer and the reflective layer are successively formed in that order on the optically transparent disk-shaped substrate (the thickness is equal to 1.2 mm for CD-R and 0.6 mm for DVD±R), and thus the optically transparent disk-shaped substrate corresponds to the optically transparent layer. In the case of BD-R, the reflective layer and the recording layer are successively formed in that order on the optical transparent disk-shaped substrate having a thickness of 1.1 mm, and a transparent cover layer having a thickness of 0.1 mm is formed on the recording layer. Thus, the transparent cover layer corresponds to the optically transparent layer.
In the optical disk as described above, heat is generated when the recording layer is irradiated with the recording laser beam to form the pits. When the generation of this heat is excessive, the shape of the pits may be deformed to a shape different from the normal shape. Technology has a reputation for being wildly unpredictable, yet there are always some who are able to forecast its path decades in advance. The Internet has been a part of our lives for over a decade, but the notion has been around for much longer. Even while streaming services have just begun taking hold in recent years, the first film was streamed over the Internet 30 years ago.
Humans are intelligent creatures, continually inventing answers to possible future issues. However, they are mostly just sketches for solutions that predicate on years of technological improvements. That being said, this hasn't prevented individuals from imagining the requirements of the future.
The Metaverse is a futuristic vision that blurs the distinction between real and virtual worlds.
It's a spiritual successor to the Internet with the ability to transform both digital and physical infrastructures. Although Facebook's recent announcements regarding the Metaverse has popularized the notion, it was first proposed in 1992, through Neal Stephenson's science-fiction novel Snow Crash.
Massive firms like Epic Games, Nvidia, Microsoft, and even digital asset exchanges like Phemex have shown their support for this idea of the Metaverse. Over the next few years, investors will pour tens of billions of dollars into making the Metaverse a reality. It might signify how our online and offline lives will become increasingly linked due to technological advancements.
Owning the New World
Some people turn to movies like 'The Matrix' and 'Ready Player One' to describe what the Metaverse will look like. In reality, no one knows how the Metaverse will turn out, just as no one fully understood what the Internet would look like in the 2000s.
This doesn’t prevent us from identifying the essentials. Although no one owns the Internet, it has spawned some of the most well-known businesses of the last two decades. Everything we've come to expect online, such as identity verification, contract employment, ads, and content production, will be transformed by the Metaverse.
It's hard to discuss the Metaverse without mentioning blockchain. Distributed networks for digital transactions are the ideal means to transfer value across digital societies. With the surge in popularity of NFTs, the Metaverse will probably be built on Web3.
The crypto industry is rapidly expanding, and as the Metaverse gains popularity in the digital world, blockchain industry executives are having some serious conversations. Jack Tao, CEO of a world famous trading platform for crypto-derivatives called Phemex, discussed the advent of the Metaverse at the World Blockchain Summit in Dubai 2021.
"The Metaverse symbolizes a new method of engaging with the digital world, one that is even more disruptive than the Internet, and one that is developed by each participant, rather than by a central authority," Tao says. He also noted that NFTs were a major driving force behind this trend's popularity.

2010 AAA 400

The 2010 AAA 400 was a NASCAR Sprint Cup Series stock car race held on September 26, 2010, at Dover International Speedway in Dover, Delaware. The 400 lap race was the twenty-eighth in the 2010 NASCAR Sprint Cup Series, as well as the second race in the ten-race Chase for the Sprint Cup, which ends the season. The race was won by Jimmie Johnson, of the Hendrick Motorsports team. Jeff Burton finished second, and Joey Logano, who started nineteenth, clinched third.

Pole position driver Jimmie Johnson maintained his lead on the first lap to begin the race, as A. J. Allmendinger, who started in the second position on the grid, remained behind him. Fourteen laps later Allmendinger became the leader of the race. Chase for the Sprint Cup participants Clint Bowyer, and Tony Stewart were in the top ten for most of the race, but in the closing laps all of them suffered spins or other problems. Afterward, Johnson became the leader of the race, once Allmendinger made a pit stop because of a loose wheel. Johnson maintained the first position to lead the most laps of 191, and to win his sixth race of the season.

There were four cautions and eighteen lead changes among ten different drivers throughout the course of the race. It was Jimmie Johnson's sixth win in the 2010 season, and the fifty-third of his career. The result moved Johnson up to second in the Drivers' Championship, thirty-five points behind Denny Hamlin and ten ahead of Kyle Busch. Chevrolet maintained its lead in the Manufacturers' Championship, thirty-five ahead of Toyota and eighty ahead of Ford, with eight races remaining in the season. A total of 88,000 people attended the race, while 3.966 million watched it on television.

The front stretch, the location of the finish line, is banked at nine degrees with the backstretch. The racetrack has seats for 135,000 spectators.

adversarial_test_results.detail: A wholly definite noun phrase ('the expensive report', 'the desk', 'the window') that contains the claimed activating token 'expensive'; the hypothesis predicts the negative pole stays at about zero, while a gradable-adjective reading fires on 'expensive'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Those findings were printed in the journal, yet the committee ignored them for months.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Definiteness carried by the demonstrative 'Those' with no indefinite, quantified or comparative phrasing anywhere; the hypothesis predicts the pole is quiet.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: These archives belong to the county, and the curator will decide on access this week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A demonstrative-marked definite text with nothing indefinite in it, testing that definiteness marked without any article token leaves the pole inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Every driver's licence lists the holder's address and the expiry date printed by the ministry.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Two possessive noun phrases and a universal quantifier ('every'), all of which the hypothesis puts on the definite side, so the pole is predicted quiet.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The title of the chapter recounts the history of the region in plain prose.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The 'of the X' construction the hypothesis names as strongly definite, twice over, with no indefinite marker to pull the preactivation negative.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Most visitors liked the stone hall, where the paintings hang near the stairs.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Most' is on the hypothesis's definite/presuppositional list and the rest of the text is definite, so the pole is predicted at about zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: This percent figure appears in the appendix of the budget report.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Puts the claimed activating token 'percent' inside a definite frame ('This percent figure', 'the budget report'); the hypothesis says definiteness governs, so this is a hard negative for the trigger-token baseline.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The teacher wrote the letter a beneath the chalk heading and stepped back.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The literal token ' a' appears as the name of a letter, not as an indefinite article, in an otherwise definite sentence; the hypothesis predicts quiet while a literal-token n-gram detector fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The keys to the cabinet hang behind the door of the staff room.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed trigger token ' to' occurs as a preposition inside a wholly definite description; the hypothesis says prepositions still sit below the line without activating the pole.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The answer will be in the appendix of the manual on the top shelf.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed trigger token ' be' appears as the copula of a definite sentence; the hypothesis predicts the pole stays near zero.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The quarterly report describes the decline of the harbour trade since spring.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The claimed token ' report' sits in a definite noun phrase with no indefinite, quantified or comparative material; predicted quiet by the hypothesis.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The 1971 report on the dock strike sits in the drawer below the atlas.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The rival-3 trigger token ' 1971' appears as an attributive numeral inside the definite noun phrase 'The 1971 report', so the hypothesis predicts quiet while number/token-identity detectors fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Several agents brought several drafts of several forms to several meetings last week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Heavily quantified text of the 'several ... several ...' kind that the hypothesis says drives the preactivation past -1.3, where the GELU dip falls back to 0.05-0.10 and the pole is predicted inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: El informe del puerto quedó sobre la mesa junto a la ventana durante toda la mañana.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A Spanish sentence that is definite throughout (el, del, la), yet contains the literal token ' a' as the preposition in 'junto a la ventana'; the hypothesis says definiteness governs, so it is predicted quiet.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The audiology literature links hearing loss with diabetes, though the mechanism has not been established. The correlation shows up in the long-running national survey, yet the reason why the condition damages the inner ear remains unexplained, and the clinicians who treat both illnesses disagree about the cause.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long passage on the diabetes and hearing-loss topic of a top example, written throughout with definite, specific reference (the mechanism, the survey, the condition, the clinicians, both illnesses) and no bare indefinite plural; the hypothesis predicts the pole stays quiet even deep into the context.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: The largest turbine drove the old ferry across the bay before dawn on Tuesday.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A definite superlative noun phrase ('The largest turbine') that a degree/comparison reading should fire on but the hypothesis treats as definite and therefore quiet.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Our accountant's report on the yard was expensive, though its summary fills only half the folder.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Three claimed trigger tokens ('report', 'yard', 'expensive') packed into a possessive, definite frame; the hypothesis predicts quiet where a trigger-token rule would fire.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A curious child once asked an unusual question about a distant star in the night sky.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A novel sentence with three indefinite noun phrases ('a curious child', 'an unusual question', 'a distant star'); the hypothesis predicts the preactivation near the GELU minimum and the pole near its ceiling.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A traveller lost a bag, and a guard found it near the gate.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Indefinite reference introduced three times mid-sentence, with no numeral or delimiter; the hypothesis predicts strong activity and the number detector does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Some of the guests left without any warning, and nobody noticed.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'Some' and 'any' are on the hypothesis's indefinite/quantified list, and 'any warning' is an unambiguous indefinite NP, so the pole is predicted active; a literal-token rule sees 'some' but a number rule does not.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: A bigger car won the race easily after the last bend of the circuit.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The indefinite twin of the 'bigger car' contrast: the hypothesis says the indefinite article makes the pole fire, while a degree/comparison reading says the comparative alone would fire even in the definite version.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: No visitors came to the museum on Monday because of the storm.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'No visitors' is quantified indefinite reference on the hypothesis's list, so the pole is predicted active even though the sentence contains no article, numeral or delimiter token for the rivals.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Any person who enters a restricted area without a permit commits an offence.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A legal-register holdout from another genre: 'Any person', 'a restricted area' and 'a permit' are all indefinite or quantified, so the hypothesis predicts activity.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Feeding stock requires care: introduce a novel feed gradually over a period of several days, and always provide roughage before any change. As with any adjustment, watch the animals closely and note a change in appetite during the first week.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long paraphrase of the animal-feed top example in which the indefinite markers ('a novel feed', 'several days', 'any change', 'a change') sit deep in the passage; the hypothesis predicts the pole fires late in the context.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Such a thing has never happened in this village, and the elders doubt it ever will.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Indefinite reference under 'such a' in an otherwise definite sentence; the hypothesis predicts the indefinite article dominates and the pole fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Dogs barked in the yard all evening and neighbours complained about the noise from the kennel.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Bare indefinite plurals ('Dogs', 'neighbours') with the claimed token 'yard': the hypothesis calls a mildly indefinite clause active, while a literal-determiner rule stays quiet on bare plurals.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Fewer guests arrived than expected, and the host ran out of chairs before the speeches.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Comparative quantifier phrasing ('Fewer ... than expected') that paraphrases the hypothesis's 'more/less X' class without using those words; the hypothesis predicts activity and the determiner rule does not.

readings.explanation: Neuron 1829's preactivation encodes the definiteness of the noun phrase being read: it is strongly positive (+0.5 to +1.2) inside definite or presuppositional reference ('the', 'this/these/those', possessives, 'each/every/all/both/most', 'of the X'), and strongly negative (-0.6 to -1.3) inside indefinite, quantified or comparative phrasing ('a/an X', 'some/any/no/several/other/another X', bare numerals, 'more/less/similar/different X'). The negative pole is the GELU dip of that signal, so its strength rises as the preactivation falls from 0, reaches the 0.17 ceiling where the preactivation sits near GELU's minimum of -0.75 (typically the token right after an indefinite article, or a mildly indefinite clause), stays at about 0 only where the whole text is definite/specific (prepositions, bare time nouns and generic verbs still dip below the activity line even there), and falls back to 0.05-0.10 where the preactivation drops past about -1.3 (heavily quantified text such as 'several ... several ...').

It is a degree/comparison neuron rather than a definiteness one: it fires on quantitative or comparative description ('more', 'less', 'similar', 'different', 'several', gradable adjectives) and its article contrast is incidental, so 'The bigger car won the race' should fire as strongly as 'A bigger car won the race'.

It is a lexical n-gram detector on the preceding determiner word: it fires whenever the literal tokens 'a', 'an', 'some', 'several', 'other' or a numeral appear in the last few tokens and is blind to definiteness marked any other way, so possessives, demonstratives, 'each/every/all' and bare plurals should leave it quiet and 'such a thing' should fire.

It is a number/token-identity detector: the pole fires on numerals and a fixed set of frequent function tokens (' 1971', '0000', 'and', ')', '%'), so a text's peak is predicted by the presence of those tokens rather than by definiteness, and 'The results were similar' should be quiet while any numeral-containing sentence fires.
